utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth; good morning interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning legal officers, court reporters, Mr. Harmon, Mr. McCloskey. I see Mr. Cayley is not here. Good morning, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic; good morning, Professor; good morning to the accused. Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even with this storm we had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed indoors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to remind you, Professor, that you are continuing under oath and you will now be answering some further questions put to you by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning; good morning, Your Honours; good morning, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. McCloskey: [cont'd]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, if we could, I'd like to go back just briefly, and if you could place the Exhibit 196 on the ELMO, the exhibit of your computer-generated graves. All right. I just want to clarify one point. I know that previously we went over the dimensions, the length, the width, and the depth of each of the secondary graves you exhumed as well as the dam, and I noticed that -- we also discussed the ramp that was present in these graves, and I wondered, could you discuss the depth, how accurate that depth figure is for these graves, how that relates to the ramp?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ramp on the Cancari 12 site which we're looking at here is at this end, and the graves get deeper as you go towards the end. That's the very nature of the machinery digging them. So the depth that I gave in my testimony on Friday relate to the maximum depths that are at the far end of the grave from the ramp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in order to determine the volume of basically the size of the grave, you would have to have the exact or a better size of the actual depth of the grave than the deepest side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't present any testimony on the volume of the grave, merely the maximum depth. The only exception to that is the grave of Zeleni Jadar, which was not dug in this way. So that was a fairly even depth all over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also in your probing of all the secondary graves, were you able to link any of the secondary graves to each over merely by this brief process of probing? Especially I'm referring -- were you able to link Cancari 3 with any of the other probed graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The content of glass at -- of broken glass at Cancari 3 and at Cancari 1 led me to think that they had both come from the same source, which I considered to be the site of Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Liplje sites. Clearly the exhumation at Liplje show these very large, cut boulders as you've described. Did you notice anything like that in the other brief probings you did on the other sides around Liplje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point about the Liplje grave is they're not boulders in the geological sense. They are actually quarried rock at Liplje, and that's unique to Liplje and to the dam site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come across any of that quarried rock as you were probing the other two Liplje sites that you probed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never seen it anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, could you -- but the probing process is not a detailed archaeological study in any way, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a detailed archaeological study, but the content at Liplje of large, fractured rocks is such that had it been present in any of the other sites, I believe I would have seen it during the scraping process at the top of the filling of the grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We hope you have a chance to get to those graves the upcoming summer. Well, let's now get on to the following summer, where you were able to look more into the Kozluk site, which you were led to, the Kozluk site, by the investigation. And you described briefly what you found there the previous summer; the area near the bottling factory, the surface remains and such. But let's put Exhibit 201 on the ELMO, if we could. If you could describe what that photo depicts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obviously an aerial photograph taken of the site of Kozluk. The area that we excavated in is this area here. This is the River Drina which forms the boundary between Republika Srpska and Serbia. This is Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record -- excuse me, Professor Wright -- the area of the exhumation was the large sort of disturbed dirt area on the left of the photo, and the area of Serbia is in the top of the photo on the other side of the Drina River from the excavation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you -- a little bit about the area and what you discovered as you excavated this particular grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first went there in 1998, when I suspected that the Cancari 3 site had come from near Kozluk. And when I went there, I found the whole area covered in soil, but in one place there were human remains. There was a leg and, I think, some other part of the anatomy, and some clothing lying around, also shell cases from rifle fire. But there was nothing else to be seen. I returned with my team in 1999, in -- I don't have the dates with me, but it was sometime in the summer, late June, July of 1999, and we brought some heavy earth-moving equipment with us. And there were three things that we discovered at Kozluk. Firstly, all traces of the burial of the bodies had been covered up by soil, and I'd like to divide the observations into three. Firstly, we discovered places where bodies had been totally removed by heavy machinery at some time before we got there. Secondly, there were places where attempts had been made to remove bodies, but my interpretation is that the attempts were given up. Some bodies had been taken away, but there were many parts of bodies that were left in the soil and then covered up again with clean soil. Thirdly, there were places that I interpret as places of execution. That is, we uncovered bodies that had -- where the executed people had dropped on the spot, and that had then been covered up with soil and had been left entirely undisturbed. My interpretation of those bodies as having dropped on the spot after being shot is based on the lack of any disturbance to the limbs, and also we recovered, by means of metal detectors, bullets embedded in the clay that was under the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have some exhibits, I think, that will help explain your conclusions, and if you could put the next exhibit, which is 202, on the ELMO. But before we get to that, let me ask, generally as you excavated this grave, did you notice this tell-tale green glass all throughout the grave fill?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there was nowhere we didn't find the green glass. I should qualify my use of the word "grave". There was little or no sign of dug graves of the sort that I have been giving testimony about. This area at Kozluk is an area of sloping ground. There are places where gravel and sand have been extracted for commercial purposes. Nearly all the bodies lay on the slopes and were then covered up with dirt. So they are graves, yes, but they are not big, excavated graves of the sort which we have been talking about in previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And if you could put Exhibit 202 on the ELMO, and if you could explain that and how that fits into the conclusions you were just speaking of.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the third type of deposit at Kozluk. This is the place where we found -- this is one of the places where we found bodies lying on a surface, this surface from which we have removed the covering dirt [indicates]. These bodies are lying individually, were originally about a metre below the surface of the soil that had covered them up. They are skeletonised because they are so close to the surface, and therefore, I decided in this case to expose the whole width of bodies. Normally, we don't do that because exposure of the fleshed bodies to oxygen causes more putrefaction. But in this case they were virtually skeletonised, so I made an exception to my normal practice. And here are bodies lying on a surface embedded in which we found many bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to clarify, your normal practice is to, as you uncover a body, you take it away so it's not open to the elements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in this case, because they were skeletonised -- and this is a good exhibit of what happened -- you just uncovered all these bodies and left them lying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, much more like a conventional archaeologically excavation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spoke of people that you thought were shot in the grave. Are those people depicted in this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the place that we called Kozluk 2 and where there's a limited number of bodies. The main area I'll talk about later of Kozluk 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about the bodies that you see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several of them in this photograph, I think about half of them, had their hands tied behind their back or their hands arranged in such a position that I believed their hands were tied behind their back. And because these bodies are so close to the surface, natural materials like cotton disintegrate as the bodies disintegrate, so in other parts of the site where the hands were behind the bodies, where they were protected from destruction, we almost invariably found ligatures, the actual ligatures themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of these bodies were actually blindfolded, were they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular photograph, I can't -- I couldn't say -- speak to the numbers, but my memory is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Kozluk grave generally there were a number of blindfolded bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Kozluk grave generally there were many blindfolded bodies, I think in the order of 16 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this photograph, can you conclude whether or not any of these individuals in the photograph were shot in the grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw injuries that are consistent with gunshot wounds, but, of course, the mortuary team determined that. But I saw, in the case of these, at least one of these individuals, a bullet embedded in bone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe yesterday [sic] You testified that you discovered bullets underneath some bodies. Was that this group or another group?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In two places we found bullets underneath bodies and this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you point out that and try to describe, on the ELMO, which bodies you're talking about, for the record. You may need to pull the photograph or the ELMO may need to come up a bit to include the entire photograph.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have an exhibit designed -- which shows the distribution of bullets coming up, but essentially they're embedded in this surface. This is the original surface that was exposed at the time of execution. It had, underneath the bodies, plant remains preserved that were actually growing in place, had been growing in place, so this was a land surface on which the people had fallen when they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And for the record, Professor Wright has pointed to the five bodies on the right side of the screen, that are separate from each other, as well as to the cluster of bodies as you move over to the left of the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At the bottom right of the illustration is a -- where the surface suddenly stops, this is an area where subsequent robbing activity took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the tooth marks and the disruption and actual removal of the bodies that are on the edge of this distribution. In other words, as you move towards the bottom right of the photograph, there is a sudden break which is where the robbing trench cut across and removed some bones from bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "tooth mark," you're talking about the tooth marks of the digging machine that robbed them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point out what you believe to be tooth marks on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on this photograph. I think they are showing in this portion, but I have another illustration to show that better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the -- where this trench comes across the bodies, were those bodies actually cut by this trenching action?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One had lost a leg by the trenching action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the next exhibit is a better exhibit on the tooth marks that you're speaking of, and that is Exhibit 132/107. That is the same group of individuals but a larger view; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at about 45 degrees the view. But we're looking at the same bodies as we looked at in the previous photographs, and the distribution from the right-hand side to the left-hand side, something like 16 or 17 bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the teeth marks on this, can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the foreground of the picture there is trench showing. It's common in these graves to find that either tyres or the teeth on the machines or both have compressed the soil at the time of the removal of the soil so that subsequent soil falls into the hollows of the tooth marks. It's much looser and it's, therefore, possible to remove it and to display the machinery that was used to do the robbing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how were you able to take the dirt off of these bodies and these scrape marks without disturbing the bodies or the scrape marks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's done in the normal archaeological way, with trowels and with brushes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your backhoe never got -- didn't get near these bodies or these scrape marks, this was all done by hand by you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is done by hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else in this photograph of interest to your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the fact that the bodies are skeletonised shows up well. Some items of synthetic clothing have survived well. The -- most of the natural materials have been destroyed by the weathering process because these bodies were quite close to the surface.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we don't see the individual number markings on these bodies that you usually photograph next to bodies, but in some other of your photographic records, each of these bodies will be identified by number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of these bodies has been assigned a sequence number, and that sequence number will be included in the photograph of each body, and that sequence number would have gone down with the body to the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this would allow us to ask the pathologist, if necessary, to identify these bodies and give us the conclusions of the autopsies of, for example, these five that are on the right-hand side of the picture?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The individual -- the bodies are treated as individual bodies for the purpose of analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For Your Honours, we have asked one of the pathologists who will testify to go over the results, particular results of these five, just for your recollection, when we get to the pathologists in a day or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned other parts of the grave. Can you discuss other parts of the grave and how that fits into your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main area of discovery of bodies is what we have called Kozluk 3, and in that area, we recovered some 270 bodies, together with about 200 body parts left over by the attempts to move some of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how you found them and any conclusions you might have reached?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are some 20 or 30 metres to the west of the picture that you have on the screen. We discovered it by scraping down the covering of soil over the bodies until we first found them and then the work changed to being done by hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do these appear to be on, like you said before, some kind of a slope?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are on a slope. They are lying on probably hundreds of thousands of pieces of broken glass. In other words, before the people were executed, the bottling factory had dumped many hundreds of broken bottles down that slope, and all 270 bodies at Kozluk 3 lie on that broken glass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever able to make any conclusions about whether or not the people were killed where they were lying or whether they were dumped there later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the margins of the distribution of the 270 bodies, where you're dealing with individual bodies at the extremities of the body mass, the bodies looked like they do in this photograph from Kozluk 3; that is, they're lying on surfaces just beyond the glassy edge, on their own, and where there are bullets embedded in the clay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the large cluster of the group? Were you able to determine anything or would that be speculation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered whether or not these people might have been shot on top of the slope and then pushed by machinery down the slope as opposed to being shot on the slope itself, on the glassy slope itself, and I wasn't able to conclude one way or the other what had happened. On the fringes of the main distribution of bodies, however, they had definitely been shot in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You found many shell casings throughout this grave, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst the bodies and to the side of the bodies, we found many shell casings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put Exhibit 203 on the ELMO and explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned in my testimony on Friday that we surveyed each of the bodies, taking 12 anatomical landmarks. This allows us to produce maps of the distribution of these bodies, of which this is the map for the site of Kozluk 3 that we've been talking about. Kozluk 3 -- in the case of Kozluk 3, the bodies had soft tissue very well preserved, and here we had to remove them as we found them, because it was the height of summer and bacterial decomposition and destruction by insects was beginning to start within two or three hours of their exposure. So we removed them one by one. Therefore, our survey is the only record that we have of what the total mass of bodies looks like, and this is a representation of the bodies at Kozluk. There are 270 complete bodies represented in this diagram. I haven't represented the body parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bodies are the little black stick figures?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the bottom left where this individual is on its own, here where its on its own you can see the effect, but, of course, within the main mass of bodies where they were sometimes four thick, you lose resolution, you lose detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the little red marks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red dots are the shell casings that we found as the bodies were removed. These are mixed up with the bodies, lying to the side of the bodies, on the surface on which the bodies lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is there anything else, any other major conclusions you wish to share with the Court? And, of course, the total number of individuals represented in the grave, as you've received information from the anthropologist, would also, of course, be important.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The anthropologist will have to testify to that, but we removed -- my records show that we moved from this location that is illustrated here some 270 bodies and some 200 body parts. I'm not aware of how many individuals the anthropologist reconstructed from these 200 body parts that are additional to the 270 shown here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just finally, Exhibit 223 is your resume or your CV, and you've had a chance to review that and that is an accurate copy of your CV; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Professor, you're now going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Visnjic, the Defence counsel, is going to ask you. Mr. Visnjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, in your statement about the exhumations in 1998, within the frameworks of your conclusions you state that none of the 857 individuals were wearing military uniforms. Can you tell us -- can you explain to us what you mean by the term "to wear military uniform"? What do you consider that term to mean in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that statement, I mean that I did not see essentially khaki jackets and khaki trousers of the sort that I associate internationally with military wear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mean that some individuals had a complete uniform or only parts of an army uniform? Is it possible that individuals were wearing both civilian and military clothing at the same time, parts of these different types of clothing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was referring to items of military clothing. I did not see, in 1998, nor in 1999, for that matter, an item of military clothing in the grave, though I have expressed in my report some caution there because the clothing is covered in mud in many instances and so the final conclusion about the nature of the clothing we found is done by the mortuary staff after washing the clothes. But I did not see, in the course of exhumations, an item of military clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same report, within your conclusions you state that on the basis of the findings by Mr. Mills, that it was possible to ascertain the time of the execution as being Thursday, the 14th of July, 1995. My question is the following: In your report, you mention that you found ten watches, eight of which are in keeping with a certain mathematical procedure and is incorporated into this term. Bearing in mind the two watches that don't fit, is it possible that in the same site, grave site, people were buried which were executed earlier on or later on and then introduced into the sites, into the graves, later on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the watches alone -- on the basis of the watches that I observed in the course of excavation, I was struck by the fact that eight out of ten showed either "Saturday 15" or "Sunday 16" in the windows. My understanding of these watches is that -- because I actually own one myself -- is that they -- you do not have to set the day or the date in order for the watch to work as a timepiece. So although one possible conclusion would be, from a watch that did not show ""Friday [sic] 15" or "Sunday 16", one possible conclusion would be that its user died at a different time. It's not a necessary conclusion, because the day and the date may never have been set.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Perhaps we could clarify which grave you're talking about. I believe that these watches are specific to specific graves, and that may make more sense.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking -- in my report, I list the -- I'm sorry, were you addressing the question to me or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. That was just an objection to try to clarify the record, because the question is vague as to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's an objection as to vagueness, because we don't know which grave site he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Visnjic, could you specify and tell us exactly what you mean in your question so that we can follow the discussion. So when you're talking about watches, perhaps it would be a good idea for you to indicate what the grave site is that you're referring to where the watches were found. Otherwise, it is difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the question -- that is to say, we are talking about two watches found at the Hodzici grave site, A-4. That is what it states in the professor's statement, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, is that precision sufficient for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Professor Wright has a whole section on the watches that he, in order to shed light on this during testimony, may want to discuss, because it doesn't make any sense if discussed without the knowledge of which watches were found in which grave, and of course each secondary grave is associated to a primary grave, and we have evidence on the record of when the primary graves were created. And so I think in order for this discussion to make sense, we need to definitely get back into the particular grave, the particular watches, because watches were found in different graves, both primary and secondary, and it's difficult to understand this particular discussion of the analysis of these particular artefacts unless we go back to the beginning, to some degree. But Professor Wright knows all about this and he can discuss it, so I merely say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Perhaps Mr. Visnjic could ask the question in a more precise way, and then Professor Wright can answer and explain. And at the end, if there are any difficulties, you can take up the matter, Mr. McCloskey, later on in your redirect. I think that that is the way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, can you tell us the following: When you located the secondary grave sites, were the aerial photographs, for your purposes and investigation, were they decisive in determining their exact locations as well as the other indicators such as the Hodzici road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aerial photographs were, in a sense, precise. But the area that they showed was an area of general disturbance, which was much larger than the grave itself. So the area of disturbance might be in the order of 100 metres by 100 metres, but within that there was a grave that might be 30 metres long and five metres -- and three metres broad. So the aerial photographs allowed us to go to the general area, but exploratory work with a backhoe had to be done to find the exact grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is linked to that answer of yours. Is it a logical assumption that underneath the larger surface that was dug, that you find the largest number of bodies? Was this assumption borne out and confirmed in practice?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do any formal analysis of the relation of the disturbed area shown by aerial images and the number of bodies. I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it was decided which of the secondary grave sites in a certain location -- let us take, for example, the Hodzici road -- would be exhumated and which did you leave for a subsequent date?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of our considerations was that we could get to the site the heavy equipment and the -- or set up the camp with washing facilities and analytical facilities and so on. Some of the sites were suitable for that, some were not. All of them, except for Hodzici 1, were by the side of a good gravel road. We decided, on the basis of the ease of work -- the separation, for instance, in Cancari road between number 12 and number 3 was a sample of two that were well separated. So there were a mixture of factors that made us decide which ones to totally exhume and which ones to probe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony yesterday [sic], you said that on the basis of your experience from Bosnia, you were able to conclude that the blue and green colour of the soil indicated that below the soil it would be probable to expect bodies. My question is the following: Based on your experience, did this refer only to the Bosnia area as a geographical region, to Bosnia itself, or -- bearing in mind the climate, the soil composition and so on, or did other factors influence you to draw that conclusion based on your previous experience?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of my own previous experience in the Ukraine, we saw dark soil associated with the bodies, but we did not see this bright green/blue soil. That is unique to my Bosnian experience, though I have read textbooks on homicide investigations, and the occurrence of such blue/green soil associated with bodies is commonly mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any differences in colour with the secondary and -- primary and secondary grave sites in terms of soil colour?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say that there were consistent differences. The primary sites that I saw were the dam -- that I investigated were the dam site, Petkovci Dam site. Around the bodies were certainly this -- around the body parts was this greenish soil. And the other primary site I have worked on is Kozluk, and again around the bodies that still had flesh associated with them was this green soil. I don't remember any differences between the general properties of the soil in those two primary sites and in the secondary sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging from your experience, what level above and below the bodies does this colouring of the soil take place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It extends to beyond the bodies, perhaps to 20 or 30 centimetres beyond the bodies, even into the undisturbed soil alongside the bodies. I should say 20 or 30 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Above and below the body level, you say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This experience of yours, does it relate -- is it the same for primary and secondary grave sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the same colouring in the soil -- would the bodies of animals produce the same soil colouring, animals or some other putrefaction, decomposition? Would it give the same soil colouring?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine that's so, but I don't have any direct experience of digging where there's a mass of animals buried. But I don't think it's something peculiar to human remains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, with respect to your experience as far as secondary grave sites are concerned, your experience in that field, what would you say determines these sites of secondary grave sites? What led the perpetrators to choose a particular secondary grave site? Was it the configuration of the soil, whether it was soft soil which would be easy to dig, or would you say there were other elements that led them to choose a particular secondary grave site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only answer I can give to that is that the sites were accessible to trucks. I can't speak for the people who dug the secondary graves, but I did observe that all of the sites could be driven to by vehicles, by heavy vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, during your testimony today in the examination-in-chief, you said that you found the bodies -- parts of bodies of two individuals at the surface of the soil in Kozluk in 1998. According to your assessment, what was the age of the body parts on that surface; that is to say, how long were they on the surface?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say, in number of years, but they still had flesh and tissue holding the bones together. They were clearly not very old. But just looking at those bones on their own, I couldn't say how old they were. The body parts, I couldn't say how old they were. Can I add to that? Now I have studied the site, I know they must be later than the executions and the main burials, because they're lying on soil that was put back over the disturbed remains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these body parts damaged in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: By definition, because they're body parts, they must have been removed from complete bodies. So to that extent they were damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what depth underneath these body parts were the rest of the bodies in the grave site located?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the exact spot where we found those body parts on the surface in 1998, immediately below that there were no other bodies. The other bodies were to the west and to the east of those two remains. There was something like 20 metres separating the site of Kozluk 2, the grave of Kozluk 2 from Kozluk 3, and they are on the surface between those two areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say whether in that locality, whether there were more exhumations at one particular spot, whether the primary gave sites were dug over several times?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that the observations we made only require one episode of robbing of the area. I didn't see any indications that led me to suggest that it had been dug over many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience, again can you exclude the possibility of there being many diggings, that is to say that the bodies had been buried many times, several times?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Kozluk, yes, because most of the bodies were totally undisturbed. It was only near the top of the main mass of the bodies that there were body parts and disturbance. Most of them were totally undisturbed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of that same report of yours, you say that a number of body parts were pulled off from the bodies during the exhumation and in the attempt to cover up the primary grave site, that they were severed from the main body. Do you know -- I know that this does not come exclusively within your field of expertise, but do you happen to know whether the pathologists, when they made the identifications, whether they discovered any of those body parts and were able to incorporate them? Did they find them in the secondary grave sites and were they able to link them up to the bodies that were found in the primary grave sites? Were they able to put two together?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're referring to the Cancari 3 site and the Kozluk site. I don't know whether they were able to fit them together. I have not been -- I have not taken part in the mortuary operation, so I don't know the results there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony today, you said that certain casings had been found below the bodies. When a bullet penetrates a human body, how deep can it go below the body and what does that depend on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a ballistics expert. I should say that the shell cases at Kozluk were found mixed up with the bodies as well as below the bodies, that is, the shell cases. The bullets were both on the edges of the Kozluk 3 site, that is, the main mass of bodies, and at Kozluk 2 were embedded in the clay below the bodies to a depth of about 5 centimetres. The shell cases were not found embedded in the clay underneath. The shell cases were found on the surface on which the bodies lay, amongst the bodies, and on top of the bodies. But I cannot -- not having any expertise in ballistics, I cannot comment on the significance of that except to say where I found them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number of bullets found, did it correspond to the number of persons executed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you if we're referring to the number of shell cases or the number of bullets?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number of bullets.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many bullets were found altogether. A lot of them will also have been found in the mortuary. And although in the site logs we recorded all the bullets found by ourselves, you would have to add to those the bullets that were found in the mortuary operation. I don't have that number with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also in your report referring to Kozluk, you stated that the bodies were transported by trucks. I think that this is to be found on page 12 of your report, just to help you. Page 12, paragraph 2, last sentence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That conclusion was based on the observations that we made in 1998, that there was a slope which had clothing and some body parts on it that -- where there were body parts spilled down the slope, and I interpreted that as being the remains of the removal of the bodies after the robbing of the primary grave. I didn't, however, see truck marks or any other evidence. That is an interpretation based on my knowledge of the Cancari 3 site, to which I attribute the bodies in the Cancari 3 site to having come from Kozluk. And knowing the road distances, I, therefore, assume they must have come by truck, and I identified at the Kozluk site a place in the landscape which had clothing and body parts and which I think is consistent with the place where the bodies were loaded into the trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, I should like to go back to your previous testimony regarding the primary grave site at the dam at Petkovci. During your examination-in-chief, you said that because of the composition of the soil, which is rocky and allows for oxygen to pass, that the putrefication of soft tissue was speeded up.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be that for the same reason, because of the circulation of air, that bodies are mummified more quickly too?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a body to become mummified, in my opinion, it has to be dry, and the site at the dam is far from dry because of the rainfall that falls on the surface of the ground. So I would not expect bodies, under those circumstances, to become mummified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the registrar to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 22/8. It is a photograph. So could it be shown to the Witness, please. I should also like to ask the registrar, Mr. President, Mr. President, to facilitate proceedings, this is a page of the transcript in which the Professor is explaining this photograph. I'm sorry, not the Professor but Mr. Ruez. Mr. Ruez was commenting on this photograph. It is page 742 of the transcript, on the 15th of March, 2000, when the investigator of the Prosecution's Office, Mr. Ruez, was explaining this photograph or, rather, Exhibit 22/8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, the part that I should like to refer to has been highlighted in yellow, and it has to do with the following: The ligatures or the cloth, as Mr. Ruez said was like a ligature, was found on the surface or immediately below the surface of the soil at the dam. My question is the following: How long is it possible for a piece of cloth of this kind to remain on the surface without decomposing, in view of the composition of the material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience of these sites is that the answer depends on the type of the material. If it's a natural material such as cotton or wool, then it is destroyed very quickly. If it's an artificial material such as nylon or polyester, then it will last for many, many years. I don't know the composition of this particular item, so I can't answer your question directly. I can only distinguish between -- in answering that general question, I can only distinguish between natural and artificial materials, and they have different -- they have different lifetimes in the soil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask for Prosecution Exhibit 131/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, excuse me for interrupting you. Are you going to use other exhibits? In that case, you can tell the registrar the exhibit numbers in advance so that she can prepare them for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I had thought about it, but in view of the fact that we didn't ask for a break between the examination-in-chief and the cross, and I'm close to ending my cross, so I think this is a more rational way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you anyway, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm having a problem finding it. If we can take a break perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I see that Mr. Harmon is going to find the exhibit for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, my question is: Is this the type of material that can last for a protracted period of time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen this material in the sites we've exhumed. I identify this as a polyester twine. Therefore, it being polyester, I would expect this to last for a protracted period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 131/1 also has a first page containing explanations, so could I ask for that to be shown to the witness as well, please. Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to display this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, can you just explain to us these two numbers that appear here in the left-hand corner, lower left-hand box?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain those numbers from my direct experience. These numbers are assigned to that object after I have handed the material over to the mortuary. So I don't know the significance of those numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, according to your report and findings, how many hand ligatures were found at the dam grave site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer that, I would have to consult my report, and then I would also have to consult the log that was taken of the remains. I have my report with me and I can have a look at that, but I do not have the log which has been tendered in evidence and is part of ICTY's records. I don't have it with me, but I will look first in my report and see if I made mention of these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, would you like a break now? Would that be convenient? We have been working for an hour and a quarter. Perhaps we could have a break now. You are about to finish, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only have one further brief question for Professor Wright, so I can put it before the break, or it's up to you. If you decide to have the break now, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, as we have questions by the Judges later, perhaps it would be better to have a break now so that Professor Wright can have a chance to look through his report. And then we can resume, because we need to have the re-examination and the questions of the Judges. So we'll now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're resuming the hearing. Mr. Visnjic, you may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, would you be so kind as to put Exhibit 22/8 onto the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, based on your experience, if we were to compare the ligature shown on this photograph, 22/8, and the ligature shown on Exhibit 131/1, the one you described earlier on, which of these two materials can have a longer lifetime on the surface of the soil?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that because I don't know the material from which this ligature was made. If it was made of polyester, then it would last a long time. If it was made of cotton, I wouldn't expect it to last very long. Can I just clarify one point too -- at one point as well, that in the testimony that I was shown, that is, in this page, the time of discovery of this item is said to be April 1998. I think it should read "April 1997", because it was found before I went to the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. Professor Wright, my next question has to do with the part of your report dealing with the potential grave site at Potocari. You carried out some investigations there, but you didn't find any bodies or remains there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in your report, if I understood you correctly, you do express a certain doubt or suspicion. So could you comment on that in a little more detail, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked to go to an area behind the bus station at Potocari where there were aerial images of disturbed soil. I looked in two of these places. In one, I could detect nothing. In the second one, a hole -- a large hole had in the past been dug and refilled, but it had no human remains in the refilling, no body parts in the refilling. What I did see near the top were some lumps of this green putrid clay, but there were no body parts adhering to them, and I am unable to come to any firm conclusion about the Potocari site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Wright. Professor, could you exclude the possibility of certain grave sites -- I'm talking about primary grave sites such as Kozluk, for instance -- after bodies had been buried there, bodies of people who were executed en masse, that there may have been additional burials of other bodies from other locations? Is this a possibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We studied the stratigraphy, that is, the layers of soil, very carefully, and I saw no evidence of subsequent burial at Kozluk. And in my opinion, that's not a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that ends my cross-examination. Professor Wright, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. McCloskey, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. Re-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wright, I believe you have Exhibit 5/22 [Realtime transcript read in error "522"], the aerial image of Potocari, and could you place that on the ELMO. So after the season of 1999, you were asked to go explore a site behind the Express bus compound in Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point, with your pointer, to the area that you actually took a look at and excavated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three areas marked by an arrow. I looked at this area, and I looked at that area, and this is the area in which I was able to identify that a large hole had been dug in the past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're referring to the area, the large hole, is the middle arrow.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The middle arrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you looked at the arrow to the bottom of the area -- of the arrow at the bottom of the picture and didn't find anything but you did find a hole under the middle arrow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how big was that hole?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to consult my report. My memory is that it was about 6 metres by 4 metres, but the dimensions are given in my report, if I may consult that. Eight metres square by 2 metres deep was my estimate of the size of that hole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to get any indication of whether it was dug by hand or dug by machine?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No direct indication, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how deep in the hole the green clay or the green soil was that you found that is usually indicative of some sort of organic body flesh?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these scattered lumps of this green clay near the top of the filling of the hole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, getting back to the watch artefacts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I apologise for interrupting you, but for the transcript, the exhibit that you showed Professor right was 5/22, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: According to my records, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I see on the LiveNote it says "522." So it needs to be corrected; 5/22.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, back to the analysis of the watches. I think if we use the example of the dam, which is, I believe, the first time in the Srebrenica case that you found and analysed a watch; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain the circumstances of finding that watch and the information that you gained in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The watch from the dam site was found as an isolated artefact within the filling of the grave, because the bodies had been mostly broken up and we were finding artefacts in the filling of the grave. This particular watch is a mechanical, automatic watch that stops about 36 to 48 hours after the last movement of the individual's wrist. If any memory serves me correctly, the watch at the dam site showed, in its day/date window, the combination of "Sunday" and "16th."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you found out the information that if it had stopped, you would just make some simple arithmetic and determine the date that it actually stopped moving; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One watch on its own, even perhaps two watches, don't take on significance. Only at the end of the season was the significance clear to me, and that is that the remarkable coincidence had taken place if these eight out of -- if all ten watches had stopped at random, the chances of eight out of ten showing either "Saturday 15" or "Sunday 16" can be simply calculated as several millions to one. So some event -- I believe some common event had caused this tendency for watches to stop on Saturday 15 or Sunday 16. That was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically you had eight watches that if you do the subtraction, would have stopped their natural movement around the -- on the 14th or 15th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were told by the investigators that there was indications that some mass executions occurred on the 14th and 15th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Rhodes told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have a question really in the light of information you gave this morning, in the testimony of this morning, as I was not present before. You mentioned that, and I quote you, "On the fringes," when you're speaking of Kozluk 3, "On the fringes of the main distribution of bodies, they had been shot in place," and they could not have been shot on the slope itself or on the top of the slope and pushed down by machinery, according to your assessment. Then speaking also of Kozluk 2, you mentioned that they had -- or some had their hands tied back, and then you mentioned later that 16 per cent were blindfolded and that none were wearing military clothes. You mentioned something like 875 were not wearing any military clothes. Some of the information I would like to base my question on, and to ask you if you are in a position to determine whether the killing or some of it took place in a fight or took place in an execution.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I can just distinguish one or two points there. The absence of military clothing that applied to 800 and something individuals is for all the sites that I have exhumed. At Kozluk there were some 280 individuals, none of whom had military clothing. At Kozluk, on the fringes of the site, I was able to conclude that the people had been shot on the spot because they lay on this vegetated surface and we found bullets embedded in this surface. In the middle of the main mass of bodies at Kozluk, because they lay on glass, on broken glass, and because bodies underneath would have absorbed some of the bullets from above, I was not able to determine directly that they had been shot on the spot, but the arrangement of the bodies is consistent with their having been shot on the spot. At Kozluk, I -- where the evidence was of a sort, where the location of the bodies was of a sort that would allow me to determine whether they had been killed on the spot or been brought from somewhere else, I concluded that they had been shot on the spot. I saw no positive evidence that the bodies had been brought from anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And being shot on the spot excludes being shot in a fight, the arrangement you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think being shot on the spot does not exclude people being shot in a fight. However, at Kozluk, 42 per cent of the 280 individuals had their hands tied behind their back, and in my opinion, that does exclude people being shot in a fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And there were no weapons -- no kind of weapons around these bodies which suggests that these people were carrying weapons or using them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, at Kozluk, any weapons whatsoever. We found the discarded shell cases from rifles and we found bullets, but I don't remember finding any weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Wright.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fuad Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Professor Wright, if you come upon a mass grave or a grave with many bodies in it, and this is to be based on your experience generally, is it possible to tell if the bodies in those graves have been put in there at different time periods? I mean maybe not within a day or so, but within weeks or months, at different time periods, or whether they were all put in there at approximately the same time.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I haven't found any graves that I have interpreted in that way. In my experience, I have two sites, one in the Ukraine and one in Bosnia that is not part of this current case, where I have concluded that bodies were put in on two occasions, but there was a small amount of time between them. At what I would expect, yes, it should be possible, because if bodies were put in, say, in -- talking generally, if they were put in in May, the month of May, and then covered up with some soil, and then more bodies were put in, that would be an indication. If they were put in in May and not covered up with soil, I would expect considerable destruction of the tissues and evidence of survival of insects and beetles, which we commonly find on bodies that have been left exposed for some time. So, yes, in general, I would be able to tell whether bodies had been put into a grave and, sometime later, new ones added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. And in the case of the bodies that you exhumed about which you testified here, did you see any such indications that bodies had been put in at significantly different times?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I saw no indications that would require me to conclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And the second part of my question is: In the case -- this would probably be primarily secondary graves -- you were able to tell, I gather from reading your report and some of the others, when bodies have come from different locations either because they have different soils or in the case of the glass; is that generally true? If a secondary grave contains bodies from two different primary sites, you would be able to tell that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should be able to tell that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Wright, I have a question of a general nature. You have seen several mass grave sites. Are you able to have an idea of the means of organisation required? Let us say the means and the organisation that was used in order to arrive at the results that you were able to observe.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have two comments to make on that. Firstly, the organisation of the digging of the grave is manifest by whether or not machinery was used. If it's dug by hand, it can be done quite casually. If it's dug by machinery, then obviously it's a bigger organisation required. My second comment is, that having related the primary graves to the secondary graves, I can conclude that the bodies were not taken by hand over several kilometres but were taken by truck, and that again bears on the question of the level of organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion and from your viewpoint, is there a difference between organisation for primary grave sites and the organisation required for secondary grave sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'd say there is a difference in level of organisation. In the case, for example, of the Kozluk site, some few hundred living people were taken there and executed. That would require much more organisation than the removal of the bodies from the Kozluk site to secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you also able to reconstruct the organisation required on the basis of the results observed for, let us say, the primary mass graves and for the secondary mass graves? Can you reconstruct -- repeat the type of organisation that was used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer to that question bears on whether or not the event took place in a very short period of time, and my conclusion at all the sites is that -- or rather I should say my conclusion at Kozluk and the secondary graves is that both operations took place over a very short period of time. The shorter the time, the greater the level of organisation required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Professor Wright, for coming here to speak before us. I should also like to thank you for cooperating with the international justice system. We thank you very much and wish you bon voyage back to your country, and every success in your continuing work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have some exhibits to tender, and they would be 188, 189 through 194, 196 through 205, and 223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, do you have any objections to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Visnjic, that it is not necessary to tender that copy of the transcript, because we have our own references, and so we have -- you have tendered the evidence and it has been admitted. What are we going to do now, Mr. McCloskey, or perhaps Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's still me. We have Dr. Bill Haglund, the chief of the exhumation season for 1996, who is a forensic anthropologist as opposed to Professor Wright, who is an archaeologist, and he will be able to tell us, much in the same vein as Professor Wright, about the exhumations and the results from 1996. He is ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have the witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe we had his exhibits ready to go, if we could put them next to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Haglund, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you. You are now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I think that you are quite familiar with procedure in the courtroom, so I can take it that you feel at ease, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And thank you for coming, to begin with. For the moment, you're going to answer questions put to you by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you state your name and spell your last?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, William D. Haglund, H-a-g-l-u-n-d.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: A forensic anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us your educational background?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. I received my Ph.D in physical anthropology at the University of Washington in Seattle, Washington State, United States.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that what was your undergraduate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: My undergraduate, I received also a masters degree in physical anthropologist and a bachelor's degree in biology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a brief outline of your employment history?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In forensics, for 16 years I was employed by the King County Medical Examiner's Office in Seattle, Washington. That's an office that has jurisdiction over all unexpected, sudden deaths; homicides; accidents; suicides; natural deaths that are unattended; and those deaths of suspicious or sudden nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was the chief medical investigator. In that position, I supervised the death scene investigators who actually went to the death scenes, the autopsy staff; and as an anthropologist, I would respond to outdoor scenes and assist police and protect our office's interests in the recovery of buried skeletal remains, scavenged remains, and remains where there were identification problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What kind of field experience have you had and employment after leaving Seattle, the Seattle office?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I took holidays and went on some foreign missions. In 1993, I was a member of the expert committee and went to Croatia. I then, on a yearly basis, once or twice a year, would go to Honduras, where I would do exhumations and identifications of individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first start working for the International Criminal Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In an official capacity, other than missions, in December 31, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe to us what the term "forensic" means and especially as it relates to anthropology, your expertise?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, let's first look at physical anthropology. Physical anthropology basically deals with the human skeleton, its development, its maturation, and how skeletons of some populations compare with other populations. The forensic physical anthropologist, also in the United States, takes courses in human genetics, archaeology, and palaeontology. Forensic anthropology is the application of that skeletal component, the development, maturation of the human skeleton to the medical-legal context, and traditionally forensic anthropologists have been called upon to identify human remains, skeletal remains usually, decomposed remains, remains where there's a question of identity. They've been asked to analyse and examine the skeleton, determine the sex, the race when appropriate, the age, stature. Sometimes we could tell about handedness, what side the person favours when they use their hands. Do interpretation of skeletal trauma, and sometimes we can tell something about how a person lived their life or what kinds of traumas they may have suffered during life. More recently, in the last two decades in the United States, forensic anthropologists have become more involved with fleshed remains, burnt remains in the autopsy setting, as well as in the recovery of remains at crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does your expertise, which is forensic anthropology, fit in with the actual exhumations which -- we've heard, as you know, from an archaeologist who's a digger. How does a bone man, an anthropologist, get involved in archaeology?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, it's a crime scene and that's part it. I do have a smattering of archaeology, but, of course, the work that we do in these sorts of teams are great endeavours with many, many people involved, and so I did have very good archaeologists working with for me and with me, Becky Saunders from the United States, Fronimis Coso [phoen] From Guatemala, and, you know, various people with other skills. So they could compensate my lack of certain skills in areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that part of your job as an anthropologist was the examination of bones, bone trauma. How did you work with the forensic pathologist? Can you explain what a forensic pathologist does and how you connect with it, realising that we're going to be hearing from some pathologists soon?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: A forensic pathologist is a medical doctor. I'm a Ph.D, Doctor of Philosophy. The forensic pathologist, of course, performs autopsy examinations and makes the medical opinion as to the cause of death. But the pathologist routinely deals with fleshed remains, and more and more as the flesh disappears and the bones come forth, the anthropologist is more involvement. So we actually compliment each other. For skeletal remains, we may assist the pathologist in the interpretation of trauma, and then they take this information from us and they incorporate it into their determination of the cause of death. But for the most part, what we're doing is reconstructing fragmented bones, putting them back together, determining the sex, the age, stature of them, the bones themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you give us a little bit, just a brief rundown on what you were doing in Rwanda before coming to Bosnia? A little bit about those projects.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. In September 1995, I did an assessment for the International Criminal Tribunal in Rwanda, for ICTR, to determine what -- of the Prosecution's priority of graves would be, lend themselves to excavation and forensic investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: And then subsequently, from the 15th of December through the 22nd of February, 1995/1996, we excavated and did the examinations on a large grave in Kibuye, Rwanda, a grave that contained or involved 496 individuals, and then another smaller forensic investigation was gone in Kigali, Rwanda. At that time, I was the forensic advisor or the ICTR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in the summer of 1995, did you come over to be in charge of the exhumations for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a person that was associated with the pathologists, can you give us a little background? We've heard about the archaeology site and the procedures there, but can you give us a little background on what happens once the bodies arrive to the morgue, especially in relation to your expertise as we'll leave some of the medical information for the pathologists?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think, as the Court appreciates, at this time the bodies arrive in varying conditions. Sometimes they're parts of bodies, sometimes they're skeletons, and sometimes they're bodies with a significant amount of flesh on them. Once the bodies -- the bodies are removed from our refrigerated containers from the numbered, sealed bags that they were regularly placed in, and they're photographed as they're opened, and then the pathologist and the radiologist look through the remains and pass them under a fluoroscope to find any projectiles that might be in the remains. Then the pathologist proceeds with their autopsy examination, removing clothing, evidence, and doing their external and internal examination. The evidence then is passed on to evidence technicians and photographers for their processing. At that time, if it's a skeletal remains, the anthropologist gets involved relatively soon doing an inventory and cleaning the bones that are necessary for us to make our determinations, or reconstructing bones. If it's a fleshed remains, then at the behest of the pathologist, we'll do any reconstruction that they wish us to do, and then we have a set group of bones which we do remove from the remains and clean and use for our estimations of sex and age, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the situation where you just have body parts and it's difficult or impossible to tell from that part alone how many people are involved, do you determine a minimum number of people from the various body parts?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. That was an issue in a few instances in 1996, but it has become a great issue since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
