utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Jose Pablo, who has dealt with these issues previous where there were many more numbers involved, I think we would like, at this point, to leave the explanation of the minimum number calculation to him. Otherwise, we'll be repeating ourselves, and it is more important to Mr. Pablo, but of course, Dr. Haglund can discuss that should the need arise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you -- we have your report which is Exhibit number 207/1, and could you open that to page 32 and place that on the ELMO so that we can see that. Now, you were speaking generally of some of the work that you do in the morgue. Can you explain that photograph and how it would have been incorporated into your work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. This is a fragmented cranium or skull minus the lower jaw, and what we've done here is placed the pieces together and glued them together. You can see there are multiple fragments. Here's one, here's one here, here's one here, and et cetera. By conjoining these fragments and putting them together, then the pathologist can look at this gunshot wound, and tell its sequence relative to other trauma that might be in the cranium and to get a better idea of entrance wounds versus exit wounds, et cetera. It helps them in their analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So an anthropologist would have assembled all these various parts and glued it together?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you point out on this particular exhibit where you see particular wounds, and describe how you know that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, this is an entrance gunshot wound. If we could just see the back side of it in a good picture, you would see that the back side of it and the direction the bullet is proceeding has a bevelled contour around the circumference of the entrance wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're referring to the skull on the upper part of the frame, the small hole?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, to the small hole here. Then there was some other trauma that went on in this, and not seeing the front, I can't appreciate what it is. But the fracture lines emanating from this gunshot wound ran like in a piece of glass. If you have one trauma to a piece of glass, the lines radiate out. If you have a subsequent trauma, the lines would radiate out but stop at the line made by the first trauma. And you see this kind of phenomena here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the bottom photograph, is that the same skull?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's the same skull, and it shows the exit wound derived from the trauma on the other side of the -- at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the kind of thing you do to assist the pathology in the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's get you to Bosnia in 1995. You did a series of exhumations of mass graves, and let's start with the first grave you did. Can you tell us a little bit about that and what you were able to conclude from the excavation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: This is looking westerly down a dirt road that runs through the Cerska Valley here. We have a high embankment down the northerly side of the road, and we have a slope or an embankment off of the southerly side of the road. Quite briefly, for 30 metres along this road there were bodies that had been placed on the surface and buried for an extension -- for about six metres down the slope. Our investigation of this site first involved looking at the surface. And on this side of the road, more dense, next to the embankment on the northerly side of the road --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you indicate, when you say "this side of the road", for the record --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: On the northerly side of the road. On the far side of the road from the grave were cartridge casings strewn along the whole 32,5-metre length where the bodies had been deposited. After clearing the vegetation from the grave on the embankment side and collecting these cartridges, we then exhumed 150 male individuals. They were men and boys. They -- 149 of them died of gunshot wounds. The majority died of multiple gunshot wounds, some of them with six, nine, and one with upwards to 20 gunshot wounds. They were all males. Their mean ages range from 14 to men in their 50s. Two of the youngest were between 11 and 15. We do their age assessments as ranges, because it's not an exact science. There were ligatures used to bind many of these individuals' wrists or arms behind their backs. We recovered 48 such ligatures. Twenty-four of those were in place, still holding the arms behind the back, and 23 were associated with other remains. I think the story that this grave tells is that 150 men and boys, maybe all at once or separately, were lined up along this side of the road; that their killers were on the opposite side of the road next to the bank; that they shot these individuals in a spraying-type fashion; that the cartridges were ejected from their weapons, where we found them and collected them from the road. And when this was done -- you can't maybe appreciate it -- but there's a large gouge of earth that has been removed by machine from this side of the road, and that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, that reflects the opposite side of the road on the left side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: On the northern side of the road. It was borrowed from the northern side of the road and used to cover up the bodies that now lay on the surface of the embankment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I understand what's the meaning of a sprayed shot, "in a spraying-type fashion" as you expressed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm using the -- coining the words of the pathologist who did this summary, about his assessment that because of the multiple gunshot wounds that covered many, many body areas, that the weapons were sort of just not aimed specifically but sort of just like this [indicates], and he called that spraying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So they were automatic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. It would be automatic weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And also for clarification I should note that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, you work in close connection with the pathologists, and you have reviewed these final summary reports of the pathologists. Unlike Professor Wright, who stopped at the grave, you're dealing with a lot of pathology issues here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. I collated the reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also assisted the pathologists, as you've shown us, with bone trauma and other issues?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, with the caveat that I'm not a medical doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This has been on ongoing debate somewhat between the two professions over the years, has it not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but I refer to medical doctors for medical opinions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you base your conclusion of the story on? Can you tell us why -- did you see any marks of heavy equipment used, or how do you know that heavy equipment was used to get soil from that side of the road?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think just a magnitude of the soil removed and the reach that would have to have been made to get the soil down, I assume it was a machine. And it's the cartridge casings -- the distribution of the cartridge casings and the fact that as this dirt was removed by the machine from the northern side of the road, many of those cartridge casings were also picked up and included in the fill of the grave, along with the bodies, and subsequently there have been some connections made, I believe, with those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell from the wire ligatures whether or not -- well, you've got 150 bodies total and about 48 wore ligatures. Were they bunched together, the 48, or were they separated throughout the grave? Can we make anything of those details?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The individuals with the ligatures were randomly disbursed in the grave above, below, and in between other bodies. As the individuals were shot, they either fell over the side or subsequently were rolled over the side. So many of them rolled further down the hill, where they piled up, and some of them still remained on the hillside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your opinion that this is a primary grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: This is a primary, undisturbed body disposal site. I think as the previous witness pointed out, technically it's not a grave, no hole was dug, but it is a repository with human remains, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you base your conclusion that it's not disturbed on?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The remains were relatively intact, as we would assume they would be, if they were deposited in that location as fleshed remains. This was a grave where decomposition was accelerated more than we would expect in deeper graves that are more protected. The decomposition was accelerated for many reasons. One, it was a shallow grave. This surface of the embankment was exposed to the sun for much of the day, which warmed up that shallow environment and then accelerated the decomposition process. The cover -- the soil and the cover was relatively gravelly, and so that it was relatively loosely compacted also. And also located on a slope like this, the drainage was very good, which also kept the remains more dry than they would if they would have been on a flat surface and other environments that we've experienced in Bosnia. So many of the remains were well advanced in decomposition and partially skeletalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, this exhibit is 16/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhumation, and that was the exhumation known at Nova Kasaba 96, since it was -- excuse me. Nova Kasaba, yes, 96. You have put what has been marked Exhibit 14/4 on, the only piece of photography we're using for this particular grave. But again can you tell us the results of the excavation and the results of your examination of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Just to orient ourselves, this is the main road, highway. We're looking at two fields, one field to the right and one field to the left [indicates]. It's separated by a hedge row of bushes. You see some light-coloured areas. These are areas of disturbance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's -- if you could just note for the record where the arrows are pointed in KS-1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, and the arrows are pointing and the letters indicate four graves, NSK -- Nova Kasaba grave number 1, grave number 2, grave number 3 and grave number 4. You can see the location of each of these graves is marked by a smear of disturbed surface soil; a very large smear on this side to the right, and to the left of the hedge, a more medium-size smear, and a very small smear up here. Nova Kasaba grave 1 was a shallow grave. It contained seven men. Nova Kasaba 2 was a deeper grave, about one and a half metres. It contained 19 men. Nova Kasaba 3 contained six men. And when I'm saying "men", men and boys, basically. I should correct myself. And Nova Kasaba 4 contained one elderly man. The seven individuals in the grave number 1 all had their hands bound behind their back. They all died of gunshot wounds. Of the 19 males recovered from Nova Kasaba 2, six -- 13 of the 19 had their hands bound behind their backs. The six -- there were six males in Nova Kasaba 3. Five of the six had their hands bound behind their back. And Nova Kasaba 4, as I previously stated, was a single individual and a skeleton. In summary, all the individuals were males. The mean age ranged from about 17 to men in their 50s. Thirty-two of the thirty-three individuals died of gunshot wounds, and there was a real bias towards gunshot wounds, multiple gunshot wounds, and gunshot wounds in the head. The 33rd individual died of massive head wounds, but according to the pathologist's report, he was unable to determine the instrument that caused that death but that the head wounds, he was sure, was the cause of the death. And 27 of the 33, again, all had their hands bound behind their backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to make -- come to any opinion regarding whether or not any of the individuals died or were shot at the location of the grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In grave number NSK-2, the grave containing the 19 individuals, some were in kneeling positions, some were in sitting positions with their heads slumped forward, and these were positions that, in my experience, would not be -- we would not encounter by individuals being thrown into a grave. It would be my opinion that they most likely were in those positions in those graves and shot in the grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to determine whether these graves were dug by hand or by machine?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They were relatively shallow graves, but the smear, the disturbed area, if we were digging graves by hand, I would expect -- for instance, the Nova Kasaba 1 grave was just probably two times bigger than the pointer size [indicates], and the grave Nova Kasaba 2 maybe covered three or four times the pointer size [indicates]. If they were dug by hand, I think we would see localised activity in the area where the grave was dug. The smear to me indicates the driving around of machinery, the movement. And this is -- gets relatively damp, and the first, oh, possibly several centimetres of this soil is muddy and churned up from this activity, and I believe that's what we're seeing. We also see tracks going into the area from the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What is that? Were you able to make out what that big area of disturbed earth is above NKS-4? It's not where the grave is pointed, but just above it there is a very large area relative of --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, that's a relatively steep embankment, and if a machine was used, it would have had to slide down there and enter it that way, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to see any indications whether this was a primary or a disturbed grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, these are all primary, undisturbed graves. And by "primary", I'm meaning that these are the graves that the individuals were placed in or were killed in and is the original position -- at the original location at which they were buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the next graves which were referred to as Lazete, and we now refer to that as Lazete in the area of Orahovac. And the first photograph is 20/2, and if you could put that on the ELMO and tell us the story of that grave.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Here we have an overview of the area of the Lazete graves. There's a main road that's traversing up from the right-hand corner towards the centre --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Haglund. We need to pull that -- look at it on your screen and centre it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I can see it just fine. Thank you. There's a road that traverses towards the centre of the picture from the upper right-hand corner. That's the main road. We see the label "Lazete 1" here, and this was noted by -- was designated by the original investigators that looked at the site. So this is a separate grave. We're interested in the grave that comes along a small rural road, crosses under a raised railroad track underpass, and is located in a field behind that raised area. So now we're looking at a large area of disturbance that directly abuts and is alongside a wooded hillside which is this dark area off to the right of the picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's designated --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: LZ-2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in the photograph. Thank you. Okay. And what can you tell us about this particular excavation and what did you find?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: This particular excavation was actually located in a drainage area where it had a very high water-table and where water ran down from the fields and the hills above it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't we look at the next exhibit, 20/8, for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: From this view now, we can see the raised railroad track bed, the underpass which you need to access this site from. The road, the little road to the farm, passes across the midline of the section running left to right here. We can see a large disturbed area here towards the centre on the right-hand side of the picture, this darker coloured area, and this is an area -- the area of disturbance that we saw on the former aerial imagery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we go to the next exhibit, which you should have before you, and could you tell us the exhibit number as it's marked on there? It should be "OTP," on the back.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It says "IT9833T."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one second. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. I'll do it myself now, thank you. OTP Exhibit 213.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Exhibit 213 is just out of your report, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct. It's an overall map that shows the Lazete 2 general area. To orient you, running from the top to the right here is the railroad embankment; again, the field road; and we're looking at the disturbed area that's outlined in blue towards the lower left-hand area of the disturbed area that we saw in the aerial imagery. You'll see one, two, three rectangular trenches which were test trenches that were dug to locate the graves. Then you see two red localised areas, and those are the graves we've designated Lazete 2A, and Lazete 2B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, do those reflect two separate pits or can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: We were unable to determine if this was a large trench that was made to deposit the remains in or if they were two separate pits. It was an unseasonably wet year in 1996, and we ran into the rainy season, which is not the best conditions under which to do some of this work, and so it did, I think, obscure some of our findings. So the answer to that question is no, that's ambiguous to us at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain those two designations and what they reflect?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. As I just said, grave A is what we call in our report LZ, Lazete 2, grave A; and Lazete 2, grave B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us about each one.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: If I might show the next exhibit. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's Exhibit 214.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if the ELMO could focus on the photograph and not at the drawing underneath. Focus and maybe blow-up on the photograph. So if we could have that photograph so it's taking up the whole screen, so we get a bit of a blow-up on it, please. Zero down on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's relatively blurred, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just go down towards it and centre it in there. It should be able to fill the screen. There we go. Okay. Whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa. Back it off a little bit so we just get the photograph.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. That's excellent. This is looking down into the grave pit. It's about a 5 by 6 metre area or mass of bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this A or B?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: This is LZ-2A. You can see individual remains, this individual here lying face up, for instance, and basically underneath this whole area are bodies below it. This is just the top layer of bodies before they've been fully exposed and removed. This mass of bodies extends to the floor of the grave, which is approximately 2 1/2 to 3 metres deep, depending on what area you measured it. It contained 112 individuals. These individuals were relatively complete remains. This whole site was -- contained these two separate assemblages of bodies, A and B. It contained one skeletal remains on the surface, and it also contained about 98 separate units of body parts, parts ranging all the way from pieces of bodies, like an arm or whatever, to bones, individuals bones and fragments of bones, and their distribution is quite telling as we go on. But this was a one single basic pile of bodies of 112 individuals. The next pile of bodies or group of bodies in the grave, LZ-2B, is significantly different. And that's Exhibit OTP 215. We'll need to back down again but not right now. What we see here, LZ-2A, was an undisturbed primary grave. Here we're looking at a disturbed primary grave. In this particular grave, what we're seeing is groups of bodies that are separated from each other. We have a group here. If we could just back off, I think, a little bit so I can get the little schematic up in the corner that would be helpful. Thank you so much. I'll move this down. This little shaded area, the shaded areas up here, represent isolated islands of human remains or bodies. So "A" would be this isolated island in the centre towards the top. "B" would be this isolated group of remains here, and on and on. We have one here towards the left. And what we see here also is that along the margins, between spaces there is no bodies at all. And along these margins, for instance, the lower boundary of "A," we see a relatively straight line. And what we have here is the evidence of bodies having been removed from the grave, removed with a machine, most likely a backhoe, a machine that would reach down into the body mass, encounter it, press them into the ground, transect whatever bodies it happened to encounter, and pull them out of the grave. So in these voids or empty spaces between where the bodies are, bodies have been removed. I might also point out the discolouration of the soil, this bluish/green discolouration that contrasts with the surrounding soil, and that's from leaching of decomposition products around these -- this group of bodies, phenomena that's been referred to, I think, previously. But if we might look closer at that individual who is extending out into the areas that the bodies have been removed from --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we have in the next exhibit a little better shot of that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. This is remains number 6, and then subsequently we'll look at remains number 13 and 14, which are under number 6. This is Exhibit 216. To help you appreciate this, this is a belt, and these are the lower extremities and pants of this individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, can we show that he's talking about the body marked number 6.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: And his legs extend into the body mass towards the upper part of the picture. Below we see his waist and his chest, and we see about the area of the breast that this body has been transected, basically chopped apart, and that the upper part, the arms and the neck and the head have, been removed from the grave. All along these sharp margins in this grave that separate groups of bodies from areas where bodies are not present, we see this phenomena; transected bodies from this removal process. When body number 6 is removed -- it was positioned right here between body 17 and 13 -- we find the same -- a similar phenomena for these bodies. In this case, this man's head and upper part of his body is still in the body group, and his legs have been severed as the body removal process removed the bodies on the other side of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you give us the basic conclusions as for numbers and blindfolds for the people in the primary undisturbed grave, Lazete 2A?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the undisturbed grave LZ-2A, had 112 individuals, and they were all males. They -- I haven't separated these all out. I think I have them as a composite. A hundred and twenty-seven of these 165 bodies from this site -- incidentally, I neglected to mention that LZ-2B has a minimum number mostly -- a minimum number of 52 people. Fifty-two plus the 112, plus the 1 skeletal remains that we found at Lazete 2 was the total of 165 individuals. Their ages range between 16 and 45 years of age. A signature of Lazete 2A and B were that there were a total of 104 blindfolds recovered from these remains. Seventy-seven blindfolded individuals were removed from grave A, and 26 or 50 per cent of the individuals in grave B were blindfolded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about cause of death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the cause of death, 158 of these 165 individuals died of gunshot wounds, in seven cases, the cause of death was undetermined, and multiple gunshot wounds accounted for wounds in 108 of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to your -- the next grave site, which you refer to as Pilica, and now we call it -- refer to it as the Branjevo Military Farm. And you're now going to Exhibit 24/4.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: This aerial imagery depicts a view of the buildings of the farm proper and surrounding fields. The buildings are labelled -- next to the road here, and they're at the mid-right of the image. Then if we proceed towards the left, past an area of brush, through the field, we come to a -- labelled a burial area, and that's the location of the grave at the Pilica grave site. The grave measured 28 by approximately 5 metres, and it ranged from 2 1/2 to 3 metres in depth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you go to the next exhibit, 217. It gives us a shot of the sort of finished product of the empty grave.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: If that could be sharpened. We're looking from one end of the grave to the other, and with these individuals standing on the floor of the grave, you can appreciate the depth of the grave, which is about in excess of 3 metres, about 3 metres. You might also appreciate -- I don't know if the colour shows up -- again this discolouration that's associated with the decomposing flesh in this environment and soil here. Although the grave space itself was 28 metres long, only 14 per cent of it was occupied, the floor space, was occupied by a pile of human remains, a minimal number of 132 individuals. Also, throughout this fill were some body parts. This gets a little complicated, but the grave itself had 53 complete individuals in this group of bodies, 23 nearly complete individuals, and another -- let's see -- hundred and -- over a hundred body parts. Actually, about 170 body parts. To give you an idea of what we were labelling as body parts, ten individuals were individuals that were missing their heads; five body part units were just upper extremities; sixteen were individuals who were transected at the torso, and so on; and then there were individual bones and bone fragments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you go to the next exhibit, 212. That also gives us an idea of the size and scope of the grave. Tell us a little bit about what this is. We need to back it off again.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well this depicts some of the -- actually, we could back off a tad more and we can see the lip of the grave. You can see the workers down in the grave, and what you can see above is the archaeologist who is doing the mapping, and at this time, the laser-generated mapping equipment is hitting a target in this pole, and we're actually delineating a body. We're measuring where the head is, where the knees are, a procedure that Dr. Wright has previously mentioned. One of the things you need to appreciate, I think, with these remains that are in deep graves that are for the most part fleshed, in fact, so well fleshed that they actually have pristine tattoos, its a very preservative environment in deep graves, but bodies are very pliable, but they're very chaotic and entangled amongst each other, with arms underneath another body and maybe legs overlapped with another body. So it's -- to remove them from the grave involves maybe reaching beneath several bodies to extract an arm and a hand, and rolling the body over so that another body could be moved out of the way and so on, and this is the process by which we need to extract them. It's not as simple as one might envision with a skeleton that's just lying there and you can expose the bones and then remove it. It's a wicked game of Pick-up Sticks, only the Pick-up Sticks, if you've ever played that childhood game, have arms and legs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you go to the next exhibit and could you explain that? It's 218. If we could zero in on the top half of that exhibit. Can you explain what this represents?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, this was a questionable luxury of having a very damp environment, that we were able to expose many bodies. Of course, when bodies are so entangled, you need to expose several surrounding a particular individual because one individual may be entwined with other individuals around them. But we see, looking down into the grave, the top of an assemblage of approximately 130 persons. We can see, for instance, the individual labelled number 3. He's lying sort of on his side with his face facing towards the upper part of the picture, so you can see his hands are bound behind his back. We have another individual over here that's bound, another one down here. All told in this group of remains, 77 people had their hands bound behind their back. To give you a little -- the ages of these people actually -- of course, they're all males, and I won't give -- when you're dealing with minimal numbers, sometimes you have more males than you do have bodies, and sometimes you have more causes of death than you have bodies, because you may have had causes of death for different parts and you don't know what parts go together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the only grouped mass of bodies in that whole grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. Like I say, it occupied -- this group of bodies occupied the far extreme of one end of the grave and the rest of the grave is empty. Just to appreciate a little bit more of the ligatures, if I may, this is also a picture that was previously shown, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 219. If we could focus on the top half of that photograph.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct. You can see in this case, this is an individual subsequently identified, and he's lying on his left side, you can see, and you can see his hands are bound at the wrists. This is an individual that has an artificial leg, and here's his hands here, bound behind his back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Then, of course, other parts of the grave had rather gruesome parts of remains. If I might just show this last exhibit, 211. This is the kind of body parts that we were finding in the grave, severed head and neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finding these kinds of severed body parts as well as this one clumped group of 132, what kind of conclusions did you reach about whether this was a disturbed or undisturbed? Can you tell us about your analysis there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think it was ambiguous. One would think --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we can turn the -- could you take that off the --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that. I think we're done, anyway, with the photographs. One of the questions that arises with these graves is why there is such a big grave space and so little of the grave occupied? That's a question I tried to answer, really not coming up with much result. The group of bodies in the pile --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Haglund. I've just been informed by my legs and by the time and colleagues it may be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I was going to draw your attention to this. I think that we need a break, a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. McCloskey, you may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, could you briefly, just to bring us back to where we were, summarise the contents of this grave, where the clusters were, where the body parts were, and then, as you were getting into, give us your analysis of what you believe that shows us?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. As I previously mentioned, this was a very large grave, 28 metres long, and at one far extremity the major portion of the remains of 132 minimal number of individuals was located. Also in this grave, in parts of it were 188 -- parts of 188 other human remains; bones, fragments, heads, et cetera. The pile, the one massive body, did have partial remains in them, mixed with them, and also in this particular mass of bodies there was vegetation and there was a soil intermixed with and amongst them. The question then is: "Was or was not the grave disturbed?" It's a large area. Only a fraction -- 14 per cent of the area of floor space of the grave was utilised. If it was not disturbed, we need to explain how bodies got dismembered and pulled apart. One possible explanation could be that the bodies were dismembered, many of them, in the process of putting them in the grave. The soil and vegetation intermixed with the remains in the major body mass would indicate to me that the bodies were probably placed into the grave by being scooped off of the ground surface in the field, where they had been killed, and maybe a front-end loader machine, and then loads of those bodies were then driven into the grave and dumped into that pile. It's possible, during that kind of process, that maybe in the scooping up of the bodies from where they lay, they could have tumbled and maybe been torn apart. That's possible. Then that might explain how, in the major body mass, you would have complete bodies and then parts of bodies, and that other parts of bodies may have been dropped along the way as the grave was being made. The other possibility is that, of course, that the grave was disturbed. We would still have an explanation for the parts of bodies in the major mass of the body mass. In this loading process, this one single group of bodies does not have the strict delineation where, you know, it looked like somebody had removed bodies and then cut them where there was a margin, as we did at the Lezete grave. But it's conceivable, like at the Lezete grave, maybe we had a large trench and piles of bodies next to each other, separated. That's another possibility, and that if the grave was then disturbed, that that mass of bodies that we did find were left behind and that the parts of bodies that we found were residual being left behind from the disturbing effort. And I think it's a bit ambiguous. Other information I've heard lends me to believe that it is a disturbed grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time you were writing your report, you didn't have access to the information regarding the secondary graves, their analysis and --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Inaudible] that information?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we do have the cluster of bodies in the bottom of that grave, and I just want to ask you, if you can, if we have a concentration of bodies similar to the cluster that we actually see in the bottom of that grave and that concentration is throughout that grave, is that grave big enough to hold 1.200 people at that concentration that we see?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, this is a rosary of "if"s, and it's rather speculative. If -- if the complete floor of the grave was packed with a density and a height of the bodies that we found in the one body mass, yes, it could hold seven to nine hundred people. But realise the grave was three metres deep. It could hold much more. But that is -- I think that tiptoes into speculation, which I don't feel I would like to warrant an opinion on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, most of your testimony has been regarding the graves and the excavation, but as a forensic anthropologist, you also supervised the morgue work and spent a lot of time helping the pathologists in actually going through the anthropology work, determining sex, age, minimum numbers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I am, Your Honours, not going to have Dr. Haglund tell us how an anthropologist determines sex and age at this point, of course, and would save that for Jose Pablo, although he can certainly answer that question if anyone would like to know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, at the end of this very long summer, did one or two of your young colleagues have some criticism regarding your supervision of the archaeology work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, there was some criticism raised regarding the perceived rate and quality of the work. Basically, that was the crux of it. The ICTY convened an expert panel to look at and interview these individuals, to look at their criticisms, and the expert panel's opinion was that the criticisms really had nothing to do with the quality, did not jeopardise the scientific quality of the work, and they added that it wasn't surprising to them to have brought together people from disparate lands and disparate backgrounds and experiences and not have some different perceptions of how things should go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And more significantly, were there -- well, did anyone -- were there any complaints regarding your work at the morgue and your anthropology work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, but there was a complain raised regarding the supervising pathologists and the autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those allegations that the supervising pathologists, in some of the reports, actually reviewed the reports and findings of other pathologists and, in some cases, changed the cause of death without notifying the underlying pathologist that did the report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I think in an effort to make things uniform. But, yes, I think it was proven he did not consult the other pathologists. And the panel, the independent expert panel, also reviewed this issue, and before they had reviewed it, I believe ICTY did take all of the original autopsy reports, the autopsy -- the ones that had been amended back to the original pathologist, to have them review it, to make sure that the autopsy reports were consistent -- the opinions were consistent with their original opinions and to verify that. And again the expert panel thought that that was an appropriate way to handle that potential misunderstanding and that there was nothing that would jeopardise the scientific validity of findings because of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you aware that the expert panel did conclude that it was inappropriate for the chief pathologist to change the reports of others without consulting them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Professor Haglund, you are now going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of the Defence. Mr. Visnjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Professor, could you tell us, in your opinion, whether the number of identified bodies is small, and what is the reason for this small number of identifications?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I've not been appraised of the actual numbers of the identifications exactly, I've not been following that issue, although I know it's proceeded far beyond what we originally had anticipated. But, yes, it's understandable to me that there are so few personal identifications if you require scientific rigorousness for positive identification. We're dealing -- if I just might give a hypothetical. If we have a small grave in a local community and we knew who should be buried in that grave, that's one kind of problem. It's easier to solve. But if you have potentially several thousand individuals and they are scattered way away from their home territory and they end up in graves that you do not know which grave who ended up in, then it becomes a great feat to interview members of 7.000 families to find them, in the first place, and then to put together a database, and then to find information enough on the bodies to help one identify them. One of the problems in these situations, of course, is that circumstantially, you may have leads to a couple of identities, but that's not a positive, to find somebody's name on a piece of paper. That just gives you an idea of who it might be. And the information that's available for these individuals, they are not fingerprints, they are not dental information, they are not hospital information, they are anecdotal information for the most part out of people's memories. And in order to scientifically identify someone, now we're left with the last resource of doing DNA identification. That's expensive and this is a great, large project. I know some progress is being made on it. But, no, I am not surprised at the small number of identifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already answered my next question, Professor. Among the bodies, was it possible, and on the basis which parameters, to establish differences between injuries that occurred during the person's lifetime and those that occurred after death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible in many, many occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also possible to ascertain with certainty, in the specific case of the grave site that you investigated, which were the injuries that may have occurred on the bodies during combat operations and those that would be the result of executions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think one has to look at a mass grave as a contextual situation, and when I look at a grave, for instance Nova Kasaba grave number 4, and I see 19 individuals in that grave, and I see that they're all shot, and I see that 13 of those individuals with their hands bound behind their backs, it defies reason to me that they would have been combat soldiers. And it's similar in the other graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question refers to this particular grave at Nova Kasaba, Nova Kasaba 4. I think one body was found there.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. It was elderly gentleman who had no determined cause of death. A skeletal remains which is explainable because of the relatively superficial nature of the body compared to the depth of the ones that were fleshed at the same site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your previous observation, can one leave open the possibility that that body may have been brought there later on and buried there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think that's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you were describing the grave Lazete 2. It seems to me that you stated, at one point, that at the top of the grave a skeleton was found.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was not over the top of the grave. It was a distance from the actual disturbed site, lying by some bushes by the hillside. We recovered it because it would not have been proper for us to leave a body lying out in the open. Whether it was actually connected with that particular incident, I could not tell, it's just that it was in the same location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of the clothing found on the bodies, is it possible to make any conclusions as to whether those bodies were those of civilians or soldiers or, rather, whether persons in civilian clothes had any traces on them which could lead to the conclusion that they were military men clothed in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't recall any indications on the remains of the people dressed in civilian clothing that they would have been military. However, in the Cerska grave, in, I believe, Lazete, and, I believe, in the Pilica grave, of all the people that were there, there may have been maybe five or so individuals that may have had -- one of them may have had military-type trousers on or maybe a jacket, something like that. But all the individuals were dressed -- of the 480 or so, the majority -- the vast majority, except for less than ten probably, were dressed in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Haglund, is one of the parameters distinguishing injuries in lifetime and after death the colour of the bones, and to what extent is that parameter important?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Excuse me. Would you repeat that? Are you asking about distinguishing trauma after death or before death; which?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The difference between those injuries before death and after death, the bone structure.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. For dried bones that have been exposed to the soil, yes, you can tell the difference between post-mortem injuries versus injuries that occurred pari-mortem or at or about the time of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is a different colour one of the elements?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, but we're dealing with bones that are completely skeletalised, and for the most part these individuals were not completely skeletalised. Many of them had very much flesh left on them. And one of the indications of trauma that occurred during life, the pathologist will find accompanying gunshot wounds, is haemorrhaging around the areas where the trauma occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your indulgence, can I have a minute, please, to consult?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Haglund, another question related to the previous one. The time factor when determining whether the injury was post-mortem or before is the time when the injuries were discovered after death, does it play a certain role?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think if you're referring to fleshed remains, I would like to defer to the medical experts, the physicians, the pathologists who deal with the fleshed remains, and that's their area of expertise. If you want to talk about bones that are skeletalised and lying in soil, then I'm happy to discourse on those, but I'd like to stay within my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're only talking about bone injuries; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In the majority of these cases they had bone injuries, but when they have injuries in the context of flesh, then I think that that's the best area for the pathologist, because some of the questions you're asking me also have to do with the characteristics of the surrounding tissue, the soft tissue, and when the anthropologist looks at bone, we clear the soft tissue away so we can see the surface of the bone, and the soft tissue is not a consideration in our analysis. That's the provenance of the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of which indicators has it been established that it was an execution, a murder, in the case of all of the bodies? Could causes of death also include suicide or combat?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I just would like again to point out that -- I have investigated many suicides. I have never seen an individual with their hands bound behind their back shoot themselves multiple times. Many of these people have multiple injuries which are totally inconsistent with the circumstances of suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I would merely point out that we also would like Dr. Haglund's CV marked as OPT Exhibit 222, which he has just provided me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will deal with all the exhibits at the end. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good morning. It's afternoon. It's morning somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In Dutch there is a word for it, but ... I have been listening carefully to your very clear testimony, and I would like just to have a few explanations. One of them concerns the body parts which you mentioned, because you said that you found once 53 complete individuals and then 170 body parts, either missing heads -- or 10 missing heads, 16 transected at the torso, and 5 upper extremities. Now, how -- and you explained that later in some way by saying that it could have been torn apart in the loading or unloading. For instance, the missing heads, ten missing heads, would they be torn apart in the loading or unloading?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It would seem more consistent -- if you mean by "unloading", you mean disturbance of the grave and removal from the grave, then it seems it would be more consistent with that than with the placing of bodies in the grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were they cut in the same way?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No. No. It was very random.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The same thing applies to the transected -- the bodies transected at the torso?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct. It was very random. If I might refer you -- I don't know what exhibit it is. It's -- the Pilica report, page 60, table 7, might help clarify some of this. Is that possible? Who might I ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's possible. If not, you might explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe you have your report with you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah. I have my report with me, and basically this is a table that summarises all 264 separate collection units that we took out of the Pilica grave, and it does mention the complete individuals of 53 and the 23 nearly completed individuals, and then it has a part called "Sections of Individuals," and there's ten bodies with missing heads. And if we looked at the individual bodies, the heads would have been taken off at different levels of the neck. It's almost like it got caught in something and then something gave way. I might say that with the fresh bodies, it's harder to transect and separate and dismember the bodies, but with bodies that are more decomposed, they come apart easier, and there are natural places in the skeleton that tend to be weaker and so they come apart. So if we went down here, we have transected torsos; missing upper extremities, lower extremities, and then we have maybe just one arm with a hand; a forearm. So it's very, very random and there's no pattern to it. It's like a mindless machine did it, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. My other question, or the last one, you said that there were many causes of death even for one body. What could these causes be?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: These were -- let's see if I can put this in a simple way. We would look at a body part, for instance. Let's say we had a head here and we had a gunshot wound to the head, and it's one of these body parts. We can say that that's a lethal gunshot wound. So that person could have died of that gunshot wound. But let's say we also had a torso and we had multiple gunshot wounds of the torso. That torso, that person whom that torso would have belonged to, could have died of those causes. Now, if those are two different people, they represent the parts of two different people, we have a cause of death for one person if we can put them together. But if we can't put them together, we have two causes of death for two body parts that could belong to the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because when you said two causes of death I thought one cause would be the cholera, another would be a gunshot, the third would be cut throat, but it is all being shot?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They are shot everywhere.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Professor Haglund, in your first account of the Cerska Valley graves, you talked about a likely scenario being that the 150 men and boys were lined up along the side after road and then they were shot by their killers from across the road, so that they all had gunshots. Some had 6 to 9, and you said one had 20. I'm wondering, even under spray shooting, under what circumstances would one of these people have gotten shot 20 times? I thought perhaps there was a hypothesis. Maybe they tried to escape or something?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My second question would be whether or not, based on all of your experience with the several grave sites, you would have any explanation or hypothesis of the fact that insofar as I can see, all but Nova Kasaba, you had basically one or in Lazete two grave sites with relatively large numbers of bodies, body parts, at least in one of the two graves. The number has been sometimes 120, 132, numbers like that. In Nova Kasaba you had a total, as I counted up, of 36 bodies but separated into four different grave sites that we saw on the aerial picture. What, if anything, would be the explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: There has subsequently been another Nova Kasaba grave that has been exhumed, and I'm not sure how many individuals -- I believe it was less than 100. I'm not sure. But I think my experience with homicides, basically, is oftentimes, although there may be some systematic approach to some killings, some are more opportunistic and you have a smaller group rather than a larger group. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I guess my question is that might be true of the killings, but if you had 36 in the same relatively small area, the fact that they went around and made four grave sites --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, that's very interesting. They may have appeared at different times. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My next questions may either be out of the area of expertise, and if it is, that's fine, or it may draw upon some of your other experiences. But one question which I find puzzling is that in these grave sites which have been disturbed, theoretically meaning that some bodies have been taken out of them, it's hard for me to hypothesise why, if somebody were intent upon concealing or getting rid of the incriminating evidence, they would take out some but leave relatively large numbers still in the grave, which would be, it seems to me, almost as incriminating. I don't know whether anything in your experience would give you any reason to figure that one out.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I assure you they don't intend to leave parts of the bodies in the graves. That's my impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You think it's done in such haste that --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think it can be done in haste. I think it could be done at night. It could be done with individuals who were not familiar with where the original graves were and of the extent of those graves. I think there's many, many possible reasonable explanations we could make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, those are some reasonable ones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Professor Haglund, I have two questions. You spoke about the disintegration of bodies, body parts and so on, and you had certain explanations. I would like try out another hypothesis for that list. Is it possible to observe this dismantling of bodies, where the trunk is transected, with regard to the process of killing by gunfire, that the transection of the bodies was related to the process in which they were killed, that is to say, gunfire or whatever?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, if we could just single out, I think, the most obvious exception, to have -- let's say bodies were transected by gunfire and then buried in the grave. It's hard for me to conceive somebody would line them up so that the feet of this one, where they were cut off, matched with the head of this one where it came off. Yes, it's possible, and in these circumstances I don't think it's probable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My other question: You spoke about, when describing the work and the composition of the teams, that there were people that had come from different countries. The team members had different experiences and different backgrounds. In your opinion, from the viewpoint of results, the results of the work, the scientific results, how do you view this difference? Was it an interesting, substantial difference; was it troubling to the work? How do you see it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a wonderful situation, to tell you the truth. I do a lot of international work, and I prefer to have international teams, and I prefer to have them not just because of their expertise, because I prefer to have different philosophical and cultural views present in a mission. In the main, the pathologists around the world read the same books. They may work under different circumstances, they may not be as well resourced or facilitated as others, but they are sound scientists. And I think to have people, as we did, from all mission countries, Switzerland, France, Denmark, Iceland, Guatemala, Peru, Chile, Canada, Great Britain, Sri Lanka, I think it's what an international tribunal is about. And the way the work is organised, the work is usually -- at least in 1996, and I think it's probably improved since then, the administration of the work, policies and protocols are established. The individuals are briefed on what those protocols are. They are made to adhere to international standards and sometimes above those international standards. The people come and they work as a team, and they work very hard and they do the best job they can, and I think the results are very credible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, if I understood you correctly, that is a conclusion -- my conclusion, but I would like to hear your opinion. The difference in heterogeneity, does it favour -- does heterogeneity favour truth better than homogeneity, from the scientific viewpoint, of course?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that the science is heterogeneous. The science, as I tried to say, is relatively uniform. These people all believe in the same science, they do the same work, they are trained in the same way, they read the same textbooks. The heterogeneity, I think in this sense, is very much, and that comes from different perspectives, different political views, different religions, different cultures. But the science itself and that forensic investigative work is fairly uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Professor. We have come to the end of your testimony. Before you go, I should like to ask Mr. McCloskey where we stand with reference to the documents and the tendering of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to offer Exhibit 211 through 219, 222, and 206 through 209. I believe those reflect all the new exhibits that we've discussed in the last two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The exhibits mentioned have been admitted into evidence. Professor Haglund, I should just like to express the gratitude of the International Tribunal for having come here and giving us the benefit of your experience, for cooperating with us, and we wish you every success in your future work. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to thank the Court for their patience, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't patience; it was a pleasure to hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, are we continuing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's now -- Mr. Cayley is ready to put on Jose Pablo Baraybar, one of the anthropologists that worked on more recent exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. We'll have the pleasure of having Mr. Cayley next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to hand to you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I think that you're quite familiar with the proceedings in the courtroom, so I take it you feel at ease. Yes. Very well. You are now going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Cayley. Please go ahead, Mr. Cayley. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned friends for the Defence. Examined by Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, good afternoon. Could you please spell your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: My name is spelled B-a-r-a-y-b-a-r.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your Christian name is Jose Pablo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were born on the 1st of October of 1964?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are of Peruvian nationality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a bachelor's degree in archaeology from the University of San Marcos in Peru; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you have a master of science degree from the University of London, in fact University College London. What was that degree; in what were your studies in?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It was a master of sciences, including many areas. I would say bio-archaelogy was one of them, the application of tendencies of human biology to archaeological human remains, as well as paleopathology, which is the study of pathological conditions in human remains, and forensics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one thing to remember, Mr. Baraybar. Because we're being simultaneously interpreted and because we're speaking the same language, you must try and speak quite slowly, and if you can pause between the end of my question and the beginning of your answer, that will help, particularly as you're using very technical terms. What year was that, your master of science degree?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you are, I think, a forensic anthropologist. Can you explain to the Court the type of work you do as a forensic anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: A forensic anthropologist deals with human remains from forensic contexts, from medical and legal contexts. Forensic anthropologists deal with the recovery and with the analysis of human remains from those kind of contexts. One of the main tasks after recovery of those remains is to ascertain the age, the sex, and the stature, among other things, of the remains recovered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, apart from your work for the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, where else have you done work as a forensic anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I have worked in Argentina, in Peru, my home country, in Haiti, Ethiopia, Congo, Guatemala. I started to work for the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, where the Forensic Unit was actually created, as a matter of fact, and from there transferred to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was all of your work as a forensic anthropologist concerned with alleged violations of human rights?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm correct in saying that from 1996 and including 1998 and 1999, you worked on exhumations in connection with the alleged events in and around Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could just be provided with Exhibit 220 and also, in fact to speed matters up, the anthropological report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, is Exhibit 220, the document marked Exhibit 220, your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I simply offer that to the Court. It contains all of Mr. Baraybar's field work, his laboratory work, his manuscripts and publications and papers in conferences and congresses. I don't intend to go through it, but I offer it to the Court as foundation for his evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, can you look at the very next document in front of you, which I think is Exhibit 233, and can you identify that document?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report I submitted last year and basically describes the anthropological examination of the human remains recovered in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying that your report is based on both exhumations and anthropology that you supervised and also is based upon the work of others, including, in fact, Dr. Haglund?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 140.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, if you could look at the top right-hand corner, there are some red index numbers, and if you could go to page 25. No, it's actually -- in fact, if the usher puts my copy on, it will make it easier. I don't want to spend time going through documents. Can that be placed on the ELMO? Mr. Baraybar, did you prepare reports on the anthropological remains of all of the graves that are actually shown on this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And let the record show that that is the ERN number page 25 up in the top right-hand corner of Exhibit 140, which is an exhibit that went through Mr. Manning. And if the usher could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Baraybar, in the case of the graves that are shaded green, which were exhumed secondary graves, did you also complete the anthropological reports on the remains from those graves?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And let the record show that the witness has confirmed on page 26, and that's the ERN number in the top right-hand corner of Exhibit 140.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your evidence earlier that the four objectives of anthropological studies of human remains are to determine the sex of the individual, to determine the age, to determine the stature, and I think you also stated to determine the minimum number of individuals within any grave. Now, purely talking in generic terms before we get to any specific grave, can you explain to the Judge how, as an anthropologist, you determine the sex of an exhumed body or human remains from a grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, the sex of a body will always be determined by an examination of external genitalia. If the body is decomposed beyond recognition or the soft tissues are virtually gone, that is not possible. Therefore, we are left with the bones to be examined. Having a complete skeleton that consists of 206 bones, we will be able to look at three different areas. In order of priority, these areas are the pelvic bones that basically are the hip bones, then the skull, and then the long bones. In each of these areas, we will be looking at a set of structures. And if the Prosecution allow me to show some illustrations, I will be able to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with the next three exhibits, which are 224, 225, and 226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I do apologise for interrupting, but you mentioned page 25, 26 of the 140 exhibit. This is just a small question, but perhaps for identification purposes we should give IT another number, because we have 926 but we also have 1026. But I'm going to leave it up to you, of course, to do that, and I do apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. Because I didn't have the document in front of me, I didn't know the -- I think it's a seven-figure number. There is, in fact, a page 26 in that document, but these were diagrams and the pages were not numbered. In fact, the only page numbers on these two pages, and I'll put them into the record, the first diagram is ERN number 00950925 and the second number is 00950926. So that will make sure that we don't confuse it with the page 26, which is a separate page but has the page number at the foot of the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, excuse me. If you could first of all show the photograph of the pelvis and explain to the Judges how you would use the pelvic bone to distinguish between a male and a female.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Right. I am showing Exhibit 224. We're looking at a male pelvis, and in order not to confuse the audience, I will avoid mentioning technical terms or the specific name of each structure. I will just point to you each of the structures we examine in order to determine a sex. If you have a complete and fully articulated pelvic bone such as in this case, you could definitely see there are a number of obvious features that will differentiate this male pelvis from the female pelvis I will show you in a moment. One of the main features is the extent of this area that I'm pointing to here. If you were to have only fragments of this pelvic bone, you would be looking at certain structures such as this one, some of the structures in this area here, primarily related to the angle of these two bones. You would be looking at some other structures not visible on this drawing, that is, basically on the inner aspect of this pubic bone. Then you will be also looking at the position and shape of the sacrum bone; that is, this one. If I may show you now a female pelvis. That is Exhibit 225. You see in this case again that this area is much, much wider in the female, primarily because it is prepared for child-bearing. Again, we would have a look at the same structure I just pointed you a moment ago, and you will see that in this case it is much wider again. We look at this angle here. That again proves to be much wider than the previous example, and to the other structures we cannot actually see in this photograph. If we continue with this observation, I will show you now a picture of a skull, a male skull, Exhibit 226. Again, the structures that will interest us are situated in the frontal bone above the nose, about -- close to the orbits, in the chin, in the area below and behind the ear, and in the area of the back of the head in the occipital bone. An observation of all these factors will allow us to determine sex. I am avoiding to show you a long bone, because that would take us quite a lot of time. However, I would like just to mention that in a long bone, we will primarily observe the rubberstisity [phoen] of the bones and take some measurements that prove to be very different between males and females.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. Just as a general question, in a case dealing specifically with your investigations in Srebrenica, where the pelvic bone was not present in mortal remains, how did you describe the sex of the individual?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We have taken a very conservative approach. In other words, whenever the pelvic bones were not present, sex was not ascertained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So am I right in saying that many of the individuals who are termed as of ascertained sex could have been males?
